newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Falling prices, rising hopes in Brazil.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Falling prices, rising hopes in Brazil.

text.p: One of Brazil's most closely watched consumer price indices posted deflation for the first time in nearly four decades, boosting hopes the country could clinch single-digit price growth in 1996.

"After this number, I'm inclined to think we could end the year in single digits," said Marcelo Audi, head of research for Merrill Lynch in Brazil. "This is much better than government and market inflation expectations, which were closer to 15 percent at the beginning of the year."

The Economic Research Institute (Fipe) said on Thursday that consumer price inflation fell 0.03 percent from November 8 through December 8. It was the first time since 1957 that Fipe registered price declines in consumer prices.
The index, which rose about 23 percent in 1995, has not posted a single-digit number since 1950.
Although Fipe only measures price activity in the greater Sao Paulo area, it is one of the most respected and closely watched of Brazil's varied consumer price indices.

Fipe was the latest in a string of indices to show negative growth in recent months. Inflation, which once soared at more than 2,000 percent a year in Brazil, has been tamed over the past two years under the government's stabilization drive known as the Real Plan.
Analysts said the Fipe number further confirmed a widely held view that Brazil was successfully making the transition from an inflation-indexed to a non-inflation indexed economy.

The latest good news, according to Fipe, was primarily due to falling food prices, which were down 0.60 percent over the previous four-week period. Declining costs for personal expenses also offset small hikes in housing, clothing, transportation, education and health costs in the Fipe index.
"Brazil has not seen this since the days of Juscelino," said Juarez Rizzieri, president of Fipe, referring to Juscelino Kubitschek, who was president of Brazil in the late 1950s.
The number surprised economists, who had expected at least a modest increase in food prices due to the holiday season.

So far this year, the Fipe consumer price index has risen by 9.86 percent. If the index closes flat or negative in December, as Fipe expects, then it would post a single-digit inflation figure for all of 1996.

The Getulio Vargas Foundation's IGP-M inflation index, which measures fluctuations in national wholesesale, consumer and construction prices, also seems set to end the year near the 10 percent mark. Through November of this year, the IGP-M index grew 8.41 percent.

Unlike in the late 1950s, however, lower inflation has come at the expense of -- not along with -- strong economic growth. And economists said the brighter inflation outlook would not mean the government could allow Brazil's economy to grow at a faster clip.

"This is something to be celebrated," Merrill's Audi said. "But it doesn't mean the government is going to ease credit because we still need to see a reversal in the trade and fiscal deficits before we see the government more agressive with economic policy."
